summary: The article describes a record number of natural disasters since January 2023 and presents Dublin, Ireland as a model of climate resilience. It covers The Emerald Barrier flood-defence project, technology such as AI sensors and cobots, the Green Tides community greening program, education initiatives like FloodHack, the Cities Above Water coalition, and the economic boost to clean tech businesses.
one_line: Dublin responds to rising sea levels with The Emerald Barrier, Green Tides, education, technology and global cooperation, becoming a model of climate resilience.
key_facts: Since January 2023 the planet has experienced a record number of natural disasters, including heatwaves across Europe and Hurricane Elara in the Caribbean.
Trinity College researchers predict sea levels in Dublin may rise as much as 1 meter by the end of this century.
Dublin launched The Emerald Barrier infrastructure project on January 3rd 2024 under Lord Mayor Siobhan Kearney.
The Emerald Barrier is a multi-billion euro project creating sea walls, surge barriers and flood gates to shield Dublin from rising waters.
Dr. Fiona Byrne oversees the technological development of The Barrier, which uses sensors, AI, predictive modeling and machine learning to forecast flood risks.
Collaborative robots (cobots) help build barriers, strengthen weak coastline points and take part in rescue operations during high tide events.
Green Tides, a citywide program unveiled on September 12, 2023, promotes roof gardens and vertical forests to absorb rainwater and reduce runoff.
Aoife Kennedy of the Green Tides program said the focus is on nurturing land so it can absorb water rather than building walls to keep it out.

Dublin City University students created the 'FloodHack' series, uniting engineers, software developers and environmental scientists to build prototype apps and devices for water management and emergency alerts.
Dublin joined the international coalition 'Cities Above Water' to share strategies and technologies among cities facing similar issues.
Kearney spoke about global solidarity at the United Nations Climate Change Conference.
Liam O'Sullivan is CEO of Dublin-based start-up AquaFortis, which develops solutions that create jobs while improving safety.
Dublin's resilience efforts have boosted clean tech and green infrastructure industries, drawing talent and investment from abroad.
